entries.411ed96869cff4981b833eeaf691b44300062641: <div sID="gen32391" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="1Tim.3" sID="1Tim.3"/> <div eID="gen32391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32392" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32393" type="x-p"/> In this chapter our apostle treats of church-officers. He specifies, I. The qualifications of a person to be admitted to the office of a bishop, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.1-1Tim.3.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. The qualifications of deacons (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8-1Tim.3.10">ver. 8-10</reference>), and of their wives (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.11">ver. 11</reference>), again of the deacons, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.12-1Tim.3.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. III. The reasons of his writing to Timothy, whereupon he speaks of the church and the foundation-truth professed therein, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14-1Tim.3.16">ver. 14, to the end</reference>.
entries.1ee698c067bc2b32d7ad7062648bd64c9420307d: <div eID="gen32393" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32392" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Duties of Bishops and Deacons. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32394" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. <hi type="super">2</hi> A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; <hi type="super">3</hi> Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; <hi type="super">4</hi> One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; 5 (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?) <hi type="super">6</hi> Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil. 7 Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. <div eID="gen32394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32395" type="x-p"/> The two epistles to Timothy, and that to Titus, contain a scripture-plan of church-government, or a direction to ministers. Timothy, we suppose, was an evangelist who was left at Ephesus, to take care of those whom the Holy Ghost had made bishops there, that is, the presbyters, as appears by <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Acts xx. 28</reference>, where the care of the church was committed to the presbyters, and they were called bishops. It seems they were very loth to part with Paul, especially because he told them they should <hi type="italic">see his face no more</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.38">Acts xx. 38</reference>); for their church was but newly planted, they were afraid of undertaking the care of it, and therefore Paul left Timothy with them to set them in order. And here we have the character of a gospel minister, whose office it is, as a bishop, to preside in a particular congregation of Christians: <hi type="italic">If a man desires the office of a bishop, he desires a good work,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen32395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32396" type="x-p"/> I. The ministry is a work. However the office of a bishop may be now thought a good preferment, then it was thought a good work. 1. The office of a scripture-bishop is an office of divine appointment, and not of human invention. The ministry is not a creature of the state, and it is a pity that the minister should be at any time the tool of the state. The office of the ministry was in the church before the magistrate countenanced Christianity, for this office is one of the great gifts Christ has bestowed on the church, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8-Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 8-11</reference>. 2. This office of a Christian bishop is a work, which requires diligence and application: the apostle represents it under the notion and character of a work; not of great honour and advantage, for ministers should always look more to their work than to the honour and advantage of their office. 3. It is a good work, a work of the greatest importance, and designed for the greatest good: the ministry is conversant about no lower concerns than the life and happiness of immortal souls; it is a good work, because designed to illustrate the divine perfections in bringing many sons to glory; the ministry is appointed to open men's eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, &c., <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Acts xxvi. 18</reference>. 4. There ought to be an earnest desire of the office in those who would be put into it; if a man desire, he should earnestly desire it for the prospect he has of bringing greater glory to God, and of doing the greatest good to the souls of men by this means. This is the question proposed to those who offer themselves to the ministry of the church of England: "Do you think you are moved by the Holy Ghost to take upon you this office?" <div eID="gen32396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32397" type="x-p"/> II. In order to the discharge of this office, the doing of this work, the workman must be qualified. 1. A minister must be blameless, he must not lie under any scandal; he must give as little occasion for blame as can be, because this would be a prejudice to his ministry and would reflect reproach upon his office. 2. He must be the husband of one wife; not having given a bill of divorce to one, and then taken another, or not having many wives at once, as at that time was too common both among Jews and Gentiles, especially among the Gentiles. 3. He must be vigilant and watchful against Satan, that subtle enemy; he must watch over himself, and the souls of those who are committed to his charge, of whom having taken the <hi type="italic">oversight,</hi> he must improve all opportunities of doing them good. A minister ought to be vigilant, because our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1 Pet. v. 8</reference>. 4. He must be sober, temperate, moderate in all his actions, and in the use of all creature-comforts. Sobriety and watchfulness are often in scripture put together, because they mutually befriend one another: <hi type="italic">Be sober, be vigilant.</hi> 5. He must be of good behaviour, composed and solid, and not light, vain, and frothy. 6. He must be given to hospitality, open-handed to strangers, and ready to entertain them according to his ability, as one who does not set his heart upon the wealth of the world and who is a true lover of his brethren. 7. Apt to teach. Therefore this is a preaching bishop whom Paul describes, one who is both able and willing to communicate to others the knowledge which God has given him, one who is fit to teach and ready to take all opportunities of giving instructions, who is himself <hi type="italic">well instructed in the things of the kingdom of heaven,</hi> and is communicative of what he knows to others. 8. No drunkard: <hi type="italic">Not given to wine.</hi> The priests were not to drink wine when they went in to minister (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.8-Lev.10.9">Lev. x. 8, 9</reference>), lest they should drink and pervert the law. 9. No striker; one who is not quarrelsome, nor apt to use violence to any, but does every thing with mildness, love, and gentleness. The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle towards all, &c., <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2 Tim. ii. 24</reference>. 10. One who is not greedy of filthy lucre, who does not make his ministry to truckle to any secular design or interest, who uses no mean, base, sordid ways of getting money, who is dead to the wealth of this world, lives above it, and makes it appear he is so. 11. He must be patient, and not a brawler, of a mild disposition. Christ, the great Shepherd and Bishop of souls, is so. Not apt to be angry or quarrelsome; as not a striker with his hands, so not a brawler with his tongue; for how shall men teach others to govern their tongues who do not make conscience of keeping them under good government themselves? 12. Not covetous. Covetousness is bad in any, but it is worst in a minister, whose calling leads him to converse so much with another world. 13. He must be one who keeps his family in good order: <hi type="italic">That rules well his own house,</hi> that he may set a good example to other masters of families to do so too, and that he may thereby give a proof of his ability to take care of the church of God: <hi type="italic">For, if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God.</hi> Observe, The families of ministers ought to be examples of good to all others families. Ministers must have their children in subjection; then it is the duty of ministers' children to submit to the instructions that are given them.—<hi type="italic">With all gravity.</hi> The best way to keep inferiors in subjection, is to be grave with them. Not having his children in subjection with all austerity, but with all gravity. 14. He must not be a novice, not one newly brought to the Christian religion, or not one who is but meanly instructed in it, who knows no more of religion than the surface of it, for such a one is apt to be lifted up with pride: the more ignorant men are the more proud they are: <hi type="italic">Lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the condemnation of the devil.</hi> The devils fell through pride, which is a good reason why we should take heed of pride, because it is a sin that turned angels into devils. 15. He must be of good reputation among his neighbours, and under no reproach from former conversation; for the devil will make use of that to ensnare others, and work in them an aversion to the doctrine of Christ preached by those who have not had a good report. <div eID="gen32397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32398" type="x-p"/> III. Upon the whole, having briefly gone through the qualifications of a gospel-bishop, we may infer, 1. What great reason we have to cry out, as Paul does, <hi type="italic">Who is sufficient for these things?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">2 Cor. ii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Hic labor, hoc opus—This is a work indeed.</hi> What piety, what prudence, what zeal, what courage, what faithfulness, what watchfulness over ourselves, our lusts, appetites, and passions, and over those under our charge; I say, what holy watchfulness is necessary in this work! 2. Have not the best qualified and the most faithful and conscientious ministers just reason to complain against themselves, that so much is requisite by way of qualification, and so much work is necessary to be done? And, alas! how far short do the best come of what they should be and what they should do! 3. Yet let those bless God, and be thankful, whom the Lord has enabled, and counted faithful, putting them into the ministry: if God is pleased to make any in some degree able and faithful, let him have the praise and glory of it. 4. For the encouragement of all faithful ministers, we have Christ's gracious word of promise, <hi type="italic">Lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>. And, if he be with us, he will fit us for our work in some measure, will carry us through the difficulties of it with comfort, graciously pardon our imperfections, and reward our faithfulness with a crown of glory that fadeth not away, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1 Pet. v. 4</reference>.
entries.260270914d5a61dcd5c52a6ce40f4aab3f32d3e9: <div eID="gen32398" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Qualifications of Deacons. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32399" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Likewise <hi type="italic">must</hi> the deacons <hi type="italic">be</hi> grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre; <hi type="super">9</hi> Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. <hi type="super">10</hi> And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being <hi type="italic">found</hi> blameless. 11 Even so <hi type="italic">must their</hi> wives <hi type="italic">be</hi> grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. <hi type="super">12</hi> Let the deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well. <hi type="super">13</hi> For they that have used the office of a deacon well purchase to themselves a good degree, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen32399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32400" type="x-p"/> We have here the character of deacons: these had the care of the temporal concerns of the church, that is, the maintenance of the ministers and provision for the poor: they served tables, while the ministers or bishops gave themselves only to the ministry of the word and prayer, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.2">Acts vi. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.6.4">4</reference>. Of the institution of this office, with that which gave occasion to it, you have an account in <reference osisRef="Acts.6.1-Acts.6.7">Acts vi. 1-7</reference>. Now it was requisite that deacons should have a good character, because they were assistants to the ministers, appeared and acted publicly, and had a great trust reposed in them. They must be <hi type="italic">grave.</hi> Gravity becomes all Christians, but especially those who are in the office in the church. <hi type="italic">Not doubled-tongued;</hi> that will say one thing to one and another thing to another, according as their interests leads them: a double tongue comes from a double heart; flatterers and slanderers are double-tongued. <hi type="italic">Not given to much wine;</hi> for this is a great disparagement to any man, especially to a Christian, and one in office, unfits men for business, opens the door to many temptations. <hi type="italic">Not greedy of filthy lucre;</hi> this would especially be bad in the deacons, who were entrusted with the church's money, and, if they were covetous and greedy of filthy lucre, would be tempted to embezzle it, and convert that to their own use which was intended for the public service. <hi type="italic">Holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, The mystery of faith is best held in a pure conscience. The practical love of truth is the most powerful preservative from error and delusion. If we keep a pure conscience (take heed of every thing that debauches conscience, and draws us away from God), this will preserve in our souls the mystery of faith. <hi type="italic">Let these also first be proved,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.10">v. 10</reference>. It is not fit that the public trusts should be lodged in the hands of any, till they have been first proved, and found fit for the business they are to be entrusted with; the soundness of their judgments, their zeal for Christ, and the blamelessness of their conversation, must be proved. Their wives likewise must have a good character (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.11">v. 11</reference>); they must be of a grave behaviour, not slanderers, tale-bearers, carrying stories to make mischief and sow discord; they must be <hi type="italic">sober and faithful in all things,</hi> not given to any excess, but trusty in all that is committed to them. All who are related to ministers must double their care to walk as becomes the gospel of Christ, lest, if they in any thing walk disorderly, the ministry be blamed. As he said before of the bishops or ministers, so here of the deacons, they must be <hi type="italic">the husband of one wife,</hi> such as had not put away their wives, upon dislike, and married others; they must <hi type="italic">rule their children and their own houses well;</hi> the families of deacons should be examples to other families. And the reason why the deacons must be thus qualified is (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.13">v. 13</reference>) because, though the office of a deacon be of an inferior degree, yet it is a step towards the higher degree; and those who had served tables well the church might see cause afterwards to discharge from that service, and prefer to serve in preaching the word and in prayer. Or it may be meant of the good reputation that a man would gain by his fidelity in this office: <hi type="italic">they will purchase to themselves great boldness in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.</hi> Observe, 1. In the primitive church there were but two orders of ministers or officers, <hi type="italic">bishops and deacons,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Phil. i. 1</reference>. After-ages have invented the rest. The office of the bishop, presbyter, pastor, or minister, was confined to prayer and to the ministry of the word; and the office of the deacon was confined to, or at least principally conversant about, serving tables. Clemens Romanus, in his epistle to the Christian (<hi type="italic">cap.</hi> 42, 44), speaks very fully and plainly to this effect, that the apostles, foreknowing, by our Lord Jesus Christ, that there would arise in the Christian church a controversy about the name <hi type="italic">episcopacy,</hi> appointed the forementioned orders, bishops and deacons. 2. The scripture-deacon's main employment was to serve tables, and not to preach or baptize. It is true, indeed, that Philip did preach and baptize in Samaria (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.4-Acts.8.25">Acts viii.</reference>), but you read that he was an evangelist (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.8">Acts xxi. 8</reference>), and he might preach and baptize, and perform any other part of the ministerial office, under that character; but still the design of the deacon's office was to mind the temporal concerns of the church, such as the salaries of the ministers and providing for the poor. 3. Several qualifications were very necessary, even for these inferior officers: <hi type="italic">The deacons must be grave,</hi> &c. 4. Some trial should be made of persons' qualifications before they are admitted into office in the church, or have any trust committed to them: <hi type="italic">Let these also first be proved.</hi> 5. Integrity and uprightness in an inferior office are the way to be preferred to a higher station in the church: <hi type="italic">They purchase to themselves a good degree.</hi> 6. This will also give a man great boldness in the faith, whereas a want of integrity and uprightness will make a man timorous, and ready to tremble at his own shadow. <hi type="italic">The wicked fleeth when no man pursueth, but the righteous are bold as a lion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>.
entries.691a3b4e490c9109b0887dbc6bc3758dcebb32a2: <div eID="gen32400" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Mystery of Godliness. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32401" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> These things write I unto thee, hoping to come unto thee shortly: <hi type="super">15</hi> But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. <hi type="super">16</hi> And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. <div eID="gen32401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32402" type="x-p"/> He concludes the chapter with a particular direction to Timothy. He hoped shortly to come to him, to give him further directions and assistance in his work, and to see that Christianity was well planted, and took root well, at Ephesus; he therefore wrote the more briefly to him. But he wrote <hi type="italic">lest he should tarry long, that</hi> Timothy <hi type="italic">might know how to behave himself in the house of God,</hi> how to conduct himself as became an evangelist, and the apostle's substitute. Observe, <div eID="gen32402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32403" type="x-p"/> I. Those who are employed in the house of God must see to it that they behave themselves well, lest they bring reproach upon the house of God, and that worthy name by which they are called. Ministers ought to behave themselves well, and to look not only to their praying and preaching, but to their behaviour: their office binds them to their good behaviour, for any behaviour will not do in this case. Timothy must know how to behave himself, not only in the particular church where he was now appointed to reside for some time, but being an evangelist, and the apostle's substitute, he must learn how to behave himself in other churches, where he should in like manner be appointed to reside for some time; and therefore it is not the church of Ephesus, but the catholic church, which is here called <hi type="italic">the house of God, which is the church of the living God.</hi> Observe here, 1. God is the living God; he is the fountain of life, he is life in himself, and he gives life, breath, and all things to his creatures; in him we live, and move, and have our being, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.25">Acts xvii. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">28</reference>. 2. The church is the house of God, he dwells there; the Lord has chosen Zion, to dwell there. "This is my rest, here will I dwell, for I have chosen it;" there may we see God's power and glory, <reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">Ps. lxiii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen32403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32404" type="x-p"/> II. It is the great support of the church that it is the church of the living <hi type="italic">God,</hi> the true God in opposition to false gods, dumb and dead idols. <div eID="gen32404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32405" type="x-p"/> 1. As the church of God, it is <hi type="italic">the pillar and ground of truth;</hi> that is, either, (1.) The church itself is the pillar and ground of truth. Not that the authority of the scriptures depends upon that of the church, as the papists pretend, for truth is the pillar and ground of the church; but the church holds forth the scripture and the doctrine of Christ, as the pillar to which a proclamation is affixed holds forth the proclamation. <hi type="italic">Even to the principalities and powers in heavenly places is made known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Eph. iii. 10</reference>. (2.) Others understand it of Timothy. He, not he himself only, but he as an evangelist, he and other faithful ministers, are the pillars and ground of truth; it is their business to maintain, hold up, and publish, the truths of Christ in the church. It is said of the apostles that <hi type="italic">they seemed to be pillars,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Gal. ii. 9</reference>. [1.] Let us be diligent and impartial in our own enquiries after truth; let us buy the truth at any rate, and not think much of any pains to discover it. [2.] Let us be careful to keep and preserve it. "<hi type="italic">Buy the truth, and sell it not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.23">Prov. xxiii. 23</reference>), do not part with it on any consideration." [3.] Let us take care to publish it, and to transmit it safe and uncorrupted unto posterity. [4.] When the church ceases to be the pillar and ground of truth, we may and ought to forsake her; for our regard to truth should be greater than our regard to the church; we are no longer obliged to continue in the church than she continues to be the pillar and ground of truth. <div eID="gen32405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32406" type="x-p"/> 2. But what is the truth which the churches and ministers are the pillars and grounds of? He tells us (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">v. 16</reference>) that <hi type="italic">without controversy great is the mystery of godliness.</hi> The learned Camero joins this with what goes before, and then it runs thus: "The pillar and ground of the truth, and <hi type="italic">without controversy great is the mystery of godliness.</hi>" He supposes this mystery to be the pillar, &c. Observe, <div eID="gen32406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32407" type="x-p"/> (1.) Christianity is a mystery, a mystery that could not have been found out by reason or the light of nature, and which cannot be comprehended by reason, because it is above reason, though not contrary thereto. It is a mystery, not of philosophy or speculation; but of godliness, designed to promote godliness; and herein it exceeds all the mysteries of the Gentiles. It is also a revealed mystery, not shut up and sealed; and it does not cease to be a mystery because now in part revealed. But, <div eID="gen32407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32408" type="x-p"/> (2.) What is the mystery of godliness? It is Christ; and here are six things concerning Christ, which make up the mystery of godliness. [1.] That he is God manifest in the flesh: <hi type="italic">God was manifest in the flesh.</hi> This proves that he is God, the eternal Word, that was made flesh and was manifest in the flesh. When God was to be manifested to man he was pleased to manifest himself in the incarnation of his own Son: <hi type="italic">The Word was made flesh,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.14">John i. 14</reference>. [2.] He is <hi type="italic">justified in the Spirit.</hi> Whereas he was reproached as a sinner, and put to death as a malefactor, he was raised again by the Spirit, and so was justified from all the calumnies with which he was loaded. <hi type="italic">He was made sin for us, and was delivered for our offences;</hi> but, being raised again, he was justified in the Spirit; that is, it was made to appear that his sacrifice was accepted, and so he rose again for our justification, as he was delivered for our offences, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Rom. iv. 25</reference>. He was put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit, <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. [3.] He was <hi type="italic">seen of angels.</hi> They worshipped him (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">Heb. i. 6</reference>); they attended his incarnation, his temptation, his agony, his death, his resurrection, his ascension; this is much to his honour, and shows what a mighty interest he had in the upper world, that angels ministered to him, for he is the Lord of angels. [4.] He is <hi type="italic">preached unto the Gentiles.</hi> This is a great part of the mystery of godliness, that Christ was offered to the Gentiles a Redeemer and Saviour; that whereas, before, salvation was of the Jews, the partition-wall was now taken down, and the Gentiles were taken in. <hi type="italic">I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.47">Acts xiii. 47</reference>. [5.] That he was <hi type="italic">believed on in the world,</hi> so that he was not preached in vain. Many of the Gentiles welcomed the gospel which the Jews rejected. Who would have thought that the world, which lay in wickedness, would believe in the Son of God, would take him to be their Saviour who was himself crucified at Jerusalem? But, notwithstanding all the prejudices they laboured under, he was believed on, &c. [6.] He was <hi type="italic">received up into glory,</hi> in his ascension. This indeed was before he was believed on in the world; but it is put last, because it was the crown of his exaltation, and because it is not only his ascension that is meant, but his sitting at the right hand of God, where he ever lives, making intercession, and has all power, both in heaven and earth, and because, in the apostasy of which he treats in the following chapter, his remaining in heaven would be denied by those who pretend to bring him down on their altars in the consecrated wafers. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He who was manifest in flesh was God, really and truly God, God by nature, and not only so by office, for this makes it to be a mystery. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God was manifest in flesh, real flesh. <hi type="italic">Forasmuch as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>. And, what is more amazing, he was manifest in the flesh after all flesh had corrupted his way, though he himself was holy from the womb. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Godliness is a mystery in all its parts and branches, from the beginning to the end, from Christ's incarnation to his ascension. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It being a great mystery, we should rather humbly adore it, and piously believe it, than curiously pry into it, or be too positive in our explications of it and determinations about it, further than the holy scriptures have revealed it to us.  <chapter eID="1Tim.3"/> <div eID="gen32408" type="x-p"/>

entries.274eec157e86d888302f9346e58ea463323a1ead: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18091"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen37215" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.1-1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:1-16</reference>. Rules as to Bishops (Overseers) AND Deacons. The Church, and the Gospel Mystery Now Revealed to It, Are the End of All Such Rules.<div eID="gen37215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18091"/>1. Translate as Greek, "Faithful is the saying." A needful preface to what follows: for the office of a bishop or overseer in Paul's day, attended as it was with hardship and often persecution, would not seem to the world generally a desirable and "good work."<div eID="gen37216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desire--</hi>literally, "stretch one's self forward to grasp"; "aim at": a distinct Greek verb from that for "desireth." What one does voluntarily is more esteemed than what he does when asked (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.15">1Co 16:15</reference>). This is utterly distinct from ambitious desires after office in the Church. (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.1">Jas 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bishop--</hi>overseer: as yet identical with "presbyter" (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.17">Ac 20:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.5-Titus.1.7">Tit 1:5-7</reference>).<div eID="gen37218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good work--</hi>literally, "honorable work." Not the honor associated with it, but the work, is the prominent thought (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.38">Ac 15:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.30">Php 2:30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.5">2Ti 4:5</reference>). He who aims at the office must remember the high qualifications needed for the due discharge of its functions. <div eID="gen37219" type="x-p"/>
entries.72b7bb51cb59123c60a1d092757d1698bc8735c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18092"/><div sID="gen37220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18092"/>2. The existence of Church organization and presbyters at Ephesus is presupposed (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.17">1Ti 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">19</reference>). The institution of Church widows (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.3-1Tim.5.25">1Ti 5:3-25</reference>) accords with this. The directions here to Timothy, the president or apostolic delegate, are as to filling up vacancies among the bishops and deacons, or adding to their number. New churches in the neighborhood also would require presbyters and deacons. Episcopacy was adopted in apostolic times as the most expedient form of government, being most nearly in accordance with Jewish institutions, and so offering the less obstruction through Jewish prejudices to the progress of Christianity. The synagogue was governed by presbyters, "elders" (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.8">Ac 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.1">24:1</reference>), called also bishops or overseers. Three among them presided as "rulers of the synagogue," answering to "bishops" in the modern sense [Lightfoot, Hebrew and Talmudic Exercitations], and one among them took the lead. Ambrose (in The Duties of the Clergy [2.13], as also Bingham [Ecclesiastical Antiquities, 2.11]) says, "They who are now called bishops were originally called apostles. But those who ruled the Church after the death of the apostles had not the testimony of miracles, and were in many respects inferior. Therefore they thought it not decent to assume to themselves the name of apostles; but dividing the names, they left to presbyters the name of the presbytery, and they themselves were called bishops." "Presbyter" refers to the rank; "bishop," to the office or function. Timothy (though not having the name) exercised the power at Ephesus then, which bishops in the modern sense more recently exercised.<div eID="gen37220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blameless--</hi>"unexceptionable"; giving no just handle for blame.<div eID="gen37221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">husband of one wife--</hi>confuting the celibacy of Rome's priesthood. Though the Jews practiced polygamy, yet as he is writing as to a Gentile Church, and as polygamy was never allowed among even laymen in the Church, the ancient interpretation that the prohibition here is against polygamy in a candidate bishop is not correct. It must, therefore, mean that, though laymen might lawfully marry again, candidates for the episcopate or presbytery were better to have been married only once. As in <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.9">1Ti 5:9</reference>, "wife of one man," implies a woman married but once; so "husband of one wife" here must mean the same. The feeling which prevailed among the Gentiles, as well as the Jews (compare as to Anna, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.36">Lu 2:36</reference>, 37), against a second marriage would, on the ground of expediency and conciliation in matters indifferent and not involving compromise of principle, account for Paul's prohibition here in the case of one in so prominent a sphere as a bishop or a deacon. Hence the stress that is laid in the context on the repute in which the candidate for orders is held among those over whom he is to preside (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">Tit 1:16</reference>). The Council of Laodicea and the apostolic canons discountenanced second marriages, especially in the case of candidates for ordination. Of course second marriage being lawful, the undesirableness of it holds good only under special circumstances. It is implied here also, that he who has a wife and virtuous family, is to be preferred to a bachelor; for he who is himself bound to discharge the domestic duties mentioned here, is likely to be more attractive to those who have similar ties, for he teaches them not only by precept, but also by example (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4">1Ti 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.5">5</reference>). The Jews teach, a priest should be neither unmarried nor childless, lest he be unmerciful [Bengel]. So in the synagogue, "no one shall offer up prayer in public, unless he be married" [in Colbo, ch. 65; Vitringa, Synagogue and Temple].<div eID="gen37222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vigilant--</hi>literally, "sober"; ever on the watch, as sober men alone can be; keenly alive, so as to foresee what ought to be done (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.6-1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:6-8</reference>).<div eID="gen37223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sober--</hi>sober-minded.<div eID="gen37224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of good behaviour--</hi>Greek, "orderly." "Sober" refers to the inward mind; "orderly," to the outward behavior, tone, look, gait, dress. The new man bears somewhat of a sacred festival character, incompatible with all confusion, disorder, excess, violence, laxity, assumption, harshness, and meanness (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Php 4:8</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen37225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apt to teach--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>). <div eID="gen37226" type="x-p"/>
entries.f73a15c05575f4be8033516cb45a84fb061a8ac3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18093"/><div sID="gen37227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18093"/><hi type="bold">3. Not given to wine--</hi>The Greek includes besides this, not indulging in the brawling, violent conduct towards others, which proceeds from being given to wine. The opposite of "patient" or (Greek) "forbearing," reasonable to others (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.4.5">Php 4:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no striker--</hi>with either hand or tongue: not as some teachers pretending a holy zeal (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Co 11:20</reference>), answering to "not a brawler" or fighter (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24">1Ki 22:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.25">Ne 13:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.4">Is 58:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.23.2">Ac 23:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2Ti 2:24</reference>, 25).<div eID="gen37228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not covetous--</hi>Greek, "not a lover of money," whether he have much or little (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">Tit 1:7</reference>). <div eID="gen37229" type="x-p"/>
entries.f90dae01c92b7fda8cf7b9325e20944c9f4f8fae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18094"/><div sID="gen37230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18094"/><hi type="bold">4. ruleth--</hi>Greek, "presiding over."<div eID="gen37230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own house--</hi>children and servants, as contrasted with "the church" (house) of God (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.5">1Ti 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">15</reference>) which he may be called on to preside over.<div eID="gen37231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having his children--</hi>rather as Greek, "having children (who are) in subjection" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen37232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gravity--</hi>propriety: reverent modesty on the part of the children [Alford]. The fact that he has children who are in subjection to him in all gravity, is the recommendation in his favor as one likely to rule well the Church. <div eID="gen37233" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a17ab4a7ed98f7dd757e9e65119350a434c33cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18095"/><div sID="gen37234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18095"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>Greek, "But."<div eID="gen37234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the church--</hi>rather, "a church" or congregation. How shall he who cannot perform the lesser function, perform the greater and more difficult? <div eID="gen37235" type="x-p"/>
entries.873c59b86fc7056fe8529718052465c80fa6b25c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18096"/><div sID="gen37236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18096"/><hi type="bold">6. not a novice--</hi>one just converted. This proves the Church of Ephesus was established now for some time. The absence of this rule in the Epistle to Titus, accords with the recent planting of the Church at Crete. Greek, "neophyte," literally, "a young plant"; luxuriantly verdant (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>). The young convert has not yet been disciplined and matured by afflictions and temptations. Contrast <reference osisRef="Acts.21.16">Ac 21:16</reference>, "an old disciple."<div eID="gen37236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lifted up with pride--</hi>Greek, literally, "wrapt in smoke," so that, inflated with self-conceit and exaggerated ideas of his own importance, he cannot see himself or others in the true light (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.4">1Ti 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.4">2Ti 3:4</reference>).<div eID="gen37237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">condemnation of the devil--</hi>into the same condemnation as Satan fell into (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">1Ti 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.26">2Ti 2:26</reference>). Pride was the cause of Satan's condemnation (<reference osisRef="Job.38.15">Job 38:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.12-Isa.14.15">Is 14:12-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.11">16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>; Jude 6). It cannot mean condemnation or accusation on the part of the devil. The devil may bring a reproach on men (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.7">1Ti 3:7</reference>), but he cannot bring them into condemnation, for he does not judge, but is judged [Bengel]. <div eID="gen37238" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cd177fc66da57c8f1b16571d08b5d7d79a55102: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18097"/><div sID="gen37239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18097"/><hi type="bold">7. a good report--</hi>Greek, "testimony." So Paul was influenced by the good report given of Timothy to choose him as his companion (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.2">Ac 16:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of them which are without--</hi>from the as yet unconverted Gentiles around (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.12">1Co 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">1Th 4:12</reference>), that they may be the more readily won to the Gospel (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>), and that the name of Christ may be glorified. Not even the former life of a bishop should be open to reproach [Bengel].<div eID="gen37240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reproach and the snare of the devil--</hi>reproach of men (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>) proving the occasion of his falling into the snare of the devil (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.9">1Ti 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.15">Mt 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.26">2Ti 2:26</reference>). The reproach continually surrounding him for former sins might lead him into the snare of becoming as bad as his reputation. Despair of recovering reputation might, in a weak moment, lead some into recklessness of living (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.12">Jr 18:12</reference>). The reason why only moral qualities of a general kind are specified is, he presupposes in candidates for a bishopric the special gifts of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>) and true faith, which he desires to be evidenced outwardly; also he requires qualifications in a bishop not so indispensable in others. <div eID="gen37241" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f041f354e3f06740adfec727acea122e67d3973: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18098"/><div sID="gen37242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18098"/>8. The deacons were chosen by the voice of the people. Cyprian [Epistle, 2.5] says that good bishops never departed from the old custom of consulting the people. The deacons answer to the chazzan of the synagogue: the attendant ministers, or subordinate coadjutors of the presbyter (as Timothy himself was to Paul, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.6">1Ti 4:6</reference>; Phm 13; and John Mark, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.5">Ac 13:5</reference>). Their duty was to read the Scriptures in the Church, to instruct the catechumens in Christian truths, to assist the presbyters at the sacraments, to receive oblations, and to preach and instruct. As the "chazzan" covered and uncovered the ark in the synagogue, containing the law, so the deacon in the ancient Church put the covering on the communion table. (See Chrysostom [19], Homily on Acts; Theophylact on Luke 19; and Balsaman on Canon 22, Council of Laodicea). The appointing of "the seven" in <reference osisRef="Acts.6.1-Acts.6.7">Ac 6:1-7</reference> is perhaps not meant to describe the first appointment of the deacons of the Church. At least the chazzan previously suggested the similar order of deacons.<div eID="gen37242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">double-tongued--</hi>literally, "of double speech"; saying one thing to this person, and another to that person [Theodoret]. The extensive personal intercourse that deacons would have with the members of the Church might prove a temptation to such a fault. Others explain it, "Saying one thing, thinking another" (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.19">Pr 20:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.13">Ga 2:13</reference>). I prefer the former.<div eID="gen37243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not greedy of filthy lucre--</hi>All gain is filthy (literally, "base") which is set before a man as a by-end in his work for God [Alford] (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.2">1Pe 5:2</reference>). The deacon's office of collecting and distributing alms would render this a necessary qualification. <div eID="gen37244" type="x-p"/>
entries.5dcf8cdf163f30cc65b1e439f2c87a8f928c1a3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18099"/><div sID="gen37245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18099"/><hi type="bold">9. the mystery of the faith--</hi>holding the faith, which to the natural man remains a mystery, but which has been revealed by the Spirit to them (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7-1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:7-10</reference>), in a pure conscience (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>). ("Pure," that is, in which nothing base or foreign is intermixed [Tittmann]). Though deacons were not ordinarily called on to preach (Stephen and Philip are not exceptions to this, since it was as evangelists, rather than as deacons, they preached), yet as being office-bearers in the Church, and having much intercourse with all the members, they especially needed to have this characteristic, which every Christian ought to have. <div eID="gen37245" type="x-p"/>
entries.f24c2132e1f1d6b0b012309f8c23f18cc16b6957: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18100"/><div sID="gen37246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18100"/>10. "And moreover," &c. [Alford].<div eID="gen37246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be proved--</hi>not by a period of probation, but by a searching inquiry, conducted by Timothy, the ordaining president (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Ti 5:22</reference>), whether they be "blameless"; then when found so, "let them act as deacons."<div eID="gen37247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blameless--</hi>Greek, "unexceptionable"; as the result of public investigation unaccused [Tittmann]. <div eID="gen37248" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ae8f0ae73048a25e72d9b7995dd56bfddc38103: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18101"/><div sID="gen37249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18101"/><hi type="bold">11. their wives--</hi>rather, "the women," that is, the deaconesses. For there is no reason that special rules should be laid down as to the wives of the deacons, and not also as to the wives of the bishops or overseers. Moreover, if the wives of the deacons were meant, there seems no reason for the omission of "their" (not in the Greek). Also the Greek for "even so" (the same as for "likewise," <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">1Ti 3:8</reference>, and "in like manner," <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1Ti 2:9</reference>), denotes a transition to another class of persons. Further, there were doubtless deaconesses at Ephesus, such as Phoebe was at Cenchrea (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.1">Ro 16:1</reference>, "servant," Greek, "deaconess"), yet no mention is made of them in this Epistle if not here; whereas, supposing them to be meant here, the third chapter embraces in due proportion all the persons in the service of the Church. Naturally after specifying the qualifications of the deacon, Paul passes to those of the kindred office, the deaconess. "Grave" occurs in the case of both. "Not slanderers" here, answers to "not double-tongued" in the deacons; so "not false accusers" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.3">Tit 2:3</reference>). "Sober" here answers to "not given to much wine," in the case of the deacons (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">1Ti 3:8</reference>). Thus it appears he requires the same qualifications in female deacons as in deacons, only with such modifications as the difference of sex suggested. Pliny, in his celebrated letter to Trajan, calls them "female ministers."<div eID="gen37249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faithful in all things--</hi>of life as well as faith. Trustworthy in respect to the alms committed to them and their other functions, answering to "not greedy of filthy lucre," <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8">1Ti 3:8</reference>, in the case of the deacons. <div eID="gen37250" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b331e3a69eb1d73d696042e98d3f561cb0f12e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18102"/><div sID="gen37251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18102"/><hi type="bold">12. husbands of one wife--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen37251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ruling their children--</hi>There is no article in the Greek, "ruling children"; implying that he regarded the having children to rule as a qualification (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.4">1Ti 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.6">Tit 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen37252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own houses--</hi>as distinguished from "the Church of God" (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.5">1Ti 3:5</reference>). In the case of the deacons, as in that of the bishops, he mentions the first condition of receiving office, rather than the special qualifications for its discharge. The practical side of Christianity is the one most dwelt on in the Pastoral Epistles, in opposition to the heretical teachers; moreover, as the miraculous gifts began to be withdrawn, the safest criterion of efficiency would be the previous moral character of the candidate, the disposition and talent for the office being presupposed. So in <reference osisRef="Acts.6.3">Ac 6:3</reference>, a similar criterion was applied, "Look ye out among you seven men of honest report." Less stress is laid on personal dignity in the case of the deacon than in that of the bishop (compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>,<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen37253" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f812ccb0f3a37ed4381e7a61f3dd088de7e1bc7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18103"/><div sID="gen37254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18103"/><hi type="bold">13. purchase to themselves a good degree--</hi>literally, "are acquiring ... a ... step." Understood by many as "a higher step," that is, promotion to the higher office of presbyter. But ambition of rising seems hardly the motive to faithfulness which the apostle would urge; besides, it would require the comparative, "a better degree." Then the past aorist participle, "they that used the office of deacon well," implies that the present verb, "are acquiring to themselves boldness," is the result of the completed action of using the diaconate well. Also, Paul would not probably hold out to every deacon the prospect of promotion to the presbytery in reward of his service. The idea of moving upwards in Church offices was as yet unknown (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.12.7">Ro 12:7</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4-1Cor.12.11">1Co 12:4-11</reference>). Moreover, there seems little connection between reference to a higher Church rank and the words "great boldness." Therefore, what those who have faithfully discharged the diaconate acquire for themselves is "a good standing-place" [Alford] (a well-grounded hope of salvation) against the day of judgment, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.19">1Ti 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13">1Co 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">14</reference> (the figurative meaning of "degree" or "step," being the degree of worth which one has obtained in the eye of God [Wiesinger]); and boldness (resting on that standing-place"), as well for preaching and admonishing others now (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>; a firm standing forth for the truth against error), as also especially in relation to God their coming Judge, before whom they may be boldly confident (<reference osisRef="Acts.24.16">Ac 24:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.28">1Jo 2:28</reference>; 3:21; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">He 4:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the faith--</hi>rather as Greek, "in faith," that is, boldness resting on their own faith.<div eID="gen37255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is in Christ Jesus--</hi>resting in Christ Jesus. <div eID="gen37256" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfa2a0475f63e17ac352d0207e89682b05bdfada: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18104"/><div sID="gen37257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18104"/><hi type="bold">14. write I ... hoping--</hi>that is, "though I hope to come unto thee shortly" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.13">1Ti 4:13</reference>). As his hope was not very confident (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>), he provides for Timothy's lengthened superintendence by giving him the preceding rules to guide him. He now proceeds to give more general instructions to him as an evangelist, having a "gift" committed to him (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shortly--</hi>Greek, "sooner," namely, than is presupposed in the preceding directions given to him. See my Introduction on this verse. This verse best suits the theory that this First Epistle was not written after Paul's visit and departure from Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.1-Acts.20.38">Ac 19:1-20:38</reference>) when he had resolved to winter at Corinth after passing the summer in Macedonia (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.6">1Co 16:6</reference>), but after his first imprisonment at Rome (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.17-Acts.28.31">Ac 28:17-31</reference>); probably at Corinth, where he might have some thoughts of going on to Epirus before returning to Ephesus [Birks]. <div eID="gen37258" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0a18bbed6d48b6197b67d6f9dcbc7b0be61d484: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18105"/><div sID="gen37259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18105"/><hi type="bold">15. But if I tarry long--</hi>before coming to thee.<div eID="gen37259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>that is, I write (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Ti 3:14</reference>) "that thou mayest know," &c.<div eID="gen37260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behave thyself--</hi>in directing the Church at Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.11">1Ti 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen37261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the house of God--</hi>the Church (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.2">He 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.6">5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.21">10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">1Co 3:16</reference>, "the temple of God"; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.22">Ep 2:22</reference>).<div eID="gen37262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is--</hi>that is, inasmuch as it is.<div eID="gen37263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the church--</hi>"the congregation." The fact that the sphere of thy functions is "the congregation of the living God" (who is the ever living Master of the house, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>, 20, 21), is the strongest motive to faithfulness in this behavior as president of a department of the house." The living God forms a striking contrast to the lifeless idol, Diana of Ephesus (<reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9">1Th 1:9</reference>). He is the fountain of "truth," and the foundation of our "trust" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Ti 4:10</reference>). Labor directed to a particular Church is service to the one great house of God, of which each particular Church is a part, and each Christian a lively stone (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the pillar and ground of the truth--</hi>evidently predicated of the Church, not of "the mystery of godliness" (an interpretation not started till the sixteenth century; so Bengel); for after two weighty predicates, "pillar and ground," and these substantives, the third, a much weaker one, and that an adjective, "confessedly," or "without controversy great," would not come. "Pillar" is so used metaphorically of the three apostles on whom principally the Jewish Christian Church depended (<reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Ga 2:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>). The Church is "the pillar of the truth," as the continued existence (historically) of the truth rests on it; for it supports and preserves the word of truth. He who is of the truth belongs by the very fact to the Church. Christ is the alone ground of the truth in the highest sense (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>). The apostles are foundations in a secondary sense (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference>). The Church rests on the truth as it is in Christ; not the truth on the Church. But the truth as it is in itself is to be distinguished from the truth as it is acknowledged in the world. In the former sense it needs no pillar, but supports itself; in the latter sense, it needs the Church as its pillar, that is, its supporter and preserver [Baumgarten]. The importance of Timothy's commission is set forth by reminding him of the excellence of "the house" in which he serves; and this in opposition to the coming heresies which Paul presciently forewarns him of immediately after (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>). The Church is to be the stay of the truth and its conserver for the world, and God's instrument for securing its continuance on earth, in opposition to those heresies (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">28:20</reference>). The apostle does not recognize a Church which has not the truth, or has it only in part. Rome falsely claims the promise for herself. But it is not historical descent that constitutes a Church, but this only, to those heresies (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Mt 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">28:20</reference>). The apostle does not recognize a Church which has not the intermediate; the "ground," or "basement" (similar to "foundation," <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>), the final support of the building [Alford]. It is no objection that, having called the Church before "the house of God," he now calls it the "pillar"; for the literal word "Church" immediately precedes the new metaphors: so the Church, or congregation of believers, which before was regarded as the habitation of God, is now, from a different point of view, regarded as the pillar upholding the truth. <div eID="gen37265" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f3ec8f054578dd5369bd0c1dedf3c48116ac900: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18106"/><div sID="gen37266" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18106"/><hi type="bold">16. And--</hi>following up <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>: The pillar of the truth is the Church in which thou art required to minister; "AND (that thou mayest know how grand is that truth which the Church so upholds) confessedly (so the Greek for 'without controversy') great is the mystery of godliness: (namely), He who (so the oldest manuscripts and versions read for 'God') was manifested in (the) flesh (He who) was justified in the Spirit," &c. There is set before us the whole dignity of Christ's person. If He were not essentially superhuman (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>), how could the apostle emphatically declare that He was manifested in (the) flesh? [Tregelles, Printed Text of the Greek New Testament]. (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.7">Php 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.2">1Jo 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>). Christ, in all His aspects, is Himself "the mystery of godliness." He who before was hidden "with God" was made manifest (<reference osisRef="John.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.4">3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.5">1Jo 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.3.8">8</reference>). "Confessedly," that is, by the universal confession of the members of "the Church," which is in this respect the "pillar" or upholder "of the truth."<div eID="gen37266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mystery--</hi>the divine scheme embodied in Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>), once hidden from, but now revealed to, us who believe.<div eID="gen37267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of godliness--</hi>rather, "piety"; a different Greek, expresses godliness (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.10">1Ti 2:10</reference>). In opposition to the ungodliness or impiety inseparable from error (departure from the faith: "doctrines of devils," "profane fables," <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.3">1Ti 6:3</reference>). To the victims of such error, the "mystery of piety" (that is, Christ Himself) remains a mystery unrevealed (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.2">1Ti 4:2</reference>). It is accessible only to "piety" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.9">1Ti 3:9</reference>): in relation to the pious it is termed a "mystery," though revealed (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7-1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:7-14</reference>), to imply the excellence of Him who is the surpassing essential subject of it, and who is Himself "wonderful" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>), surpassing knowledge (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.18">Ep 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">19</reference>); compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">Ep 5:32</reference>. The apostle now proceeds to unfold this confessedly great mystery in its details. It is not unlikely that some formula of confession or hymn existed in the Church and was generally accepted, to which Paul alludes in the words "confessedly great is the mystery," &c. (to wit), "He who was manifested," &c. Such hymns were then used (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.19">Ep 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>). Pliny [1.10, Epistle, 97], "They are wont on a fixed day before dawn to meet and sing a hymn in alternate responses to Christ, as being God"; and Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 5.28]. The short unconnected sentences with the words similarly arranged, and the number of syllables almost equal, and the ideas antithetically related, are characteristics of a Christian hymn. The clauses stand in parallelism; each two are connected as a pair, and form an antithesis turning on the opposition of heaven to earth; the order of this antithesis is reversed in each new pair of clauses: flesh and spirit, angels and Gentiles, world and glory; and there is a correspondence between the first and the last clause: "manifested in the flesh, received up into glory" [Wiesinger].<div eID="gen37268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">justified--</hi>that is, approved to be righteous [Alford]. Christ, while "in the flesh," seemed to be just such a one as men in the flesh, and in fact bore their sins; but by having died to sin, and having risen again, He gained for Himself and His people justifying righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.8">Is 50:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.10">Joh 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.14">Ac 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.7">6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1Pe 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.1">4:1</reference> <reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>) [Bengel]; or rather, as the antithesis to "was manifest in the flesh" requires, He was justified in the Spirit at the same time that He was manifest in the flesh, that is, He was vindicated as divine "in His Spirit," that is, in His higher nature; in contrast to "in the flesh," His visible human nature. This contrasted opposition requires "in the Spirit" to be thus explained: not "by the Spirit," as Alford explains it. So <reference osisRef="Rom.1.3">Ro 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>, "Made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead." So "justified" is used to mean vindicated in one's true character (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.19">Mt 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.7.35">Lu 7:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Ro 3:4</reference>). His manifestation "in the flesh" exposed him to misapprehension, as though he were nothing more (<reference osisRef="John.6.41">Joh 6:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.27">7:27</reference>). His justification, or vindication, in respect to His Spirit or higher being, was effected by ALL that manifested that higher being, His words (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.29">Mt 7:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.46">Joh 7:46</reference>), His works (<reference osisRef="John.2.11">Joh 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">3:2</reference>), by His Father's testimony at His baptism (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>), and at the transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">Mt 17:5</reference>), and especially by His resurrection (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Ac 13:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>), though not by this exclusively, as Bengel limits it.<div eID="gen37269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen of angels--</hi>answering to "preached unto the Gentiles" (or rather "among the nations"; including the Jews), on the other hand (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">Mt 28:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.26">26</reference>). "Angels saw the Son of God with us, not having seen Him before" [Chrysostom].' "not even they had seen His divine nature, which is not visible to any creature, but they saw Him incarnate" [Theodoret] (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Ep 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.12">1Pe 1:12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). What angels came to know by seeing, the nations learned by preaching. He is a new message to the one class as well as to the other; in the wondrous union in His person of things most opposite, namely, heaven and earth, lies "the mystery" [Wiesinger]. If the English Version, "Gentiles," be retained, the antithesis will be between the angels who are so near the Son of God, the Lord of "angels," and the Gentiles who were so utterly "afar off" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>).<div eID="gen37270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believed on in the world--</hi>which lieth in wickedness (<reference osisRef="1John.2.15">1Jo 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">5:19</reference>). Opposed to "glory" (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.17">17</reference>). This followed upon His being "preached" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.14">Ro 10:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">received up into glory--</hi>Greek, "in glory." However, English Version may be retained thus, "Received up (so as now to be) in glory," that is, into glory (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.19">Mr 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.24.51">Lu 24:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>). His reception in heaven answers to His reception on earth by being "believed on." <chapter eID="1Tim.3"/>

entries.2b423daf58d3ae0e02d80bf2890ec4362aedf23a: <div eID="gen51618" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51619" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51620" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51620" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51619" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51621" type="x-p"/> Concerning bishops, their qualifications and work, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.1-1Tim.3.7">1Tim 3:1-7</reference>. Of deacons, and how they should be proved, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.8-1Tim.3.10">1Tim 3:8-10</reference>. Of their wives and children, and how they should be governed, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.11-1Tim.3.13">1Tim 3:11-13</reference>. How Timothy should behave himself in the Church, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.14">1Tim 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Tim 3:15</reference>. The great mystery of godliness, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Tim 3:16</reference>. <div eID="gen51621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51623" type="x-p"/> This is a true saying - Πιστος ὁ λογος· This is a true doctrine. These words are joined to the last verse of the preceding chapter by several of the Greek fathers, and by them referred to the doctrine there stated. <div eID="gen51623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51624" type="x-p"/> The office of a bishop - Επισκοπης· The episcopacy, overseership or superintendency. The word ορεγεται, which we translate desire, signifies earnest, eager, passionate desire; and επιθυμει, which we translate desire, also signifies earnestly to desire or covet. It is strange that the episcopacy, in those times, should have been an object of intense desire to any man; when it was a place of danger, awl exposure to severe labor, want, persecution, and death, without any secular emolument whatsoever. On this ground I am led to think that the Spirit of God designed these words more for the ages that were to come, than for those which were then; and in reference to after ages the whole of what follows is chiefly to be understood. <div eID="gen51624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51625" type="x-p"/> A good work - A work it then was; heavy, incessant, and painful. There were no unpreaching prelates in those days, and should be none now. Episcopacy in the Church of God is of Divine appointment, and should be maintained and respected. Under God, there should be supreme governors in the Church as well as in the state. The state has its monarch, the Church has its bishop; one should govern according to the laws of the land, the other according to the word of God. <div eID="gen51625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51626" type="x-p"/> What a constitutional king should be, the principles of the constitution declare; what a bishop should be, the following verses particularly show.
entries.5b77c21a9db4987cdf7a567482628a2828b8a1f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51627" type="x-p"/> A bishop then must be blameless - Our term bishop comes from the Anglo-Saxon, which is a mere corruption of the Greek επισκοπος, and the Latin episcopus; the former being compounded of επι, over, and σκεπτομαι, to look or inspect, signifies one who has the inspection or oversight of a place, persons, or business; what we commonly term a superintendent. The New Testament writers have borrowed the term from the Septuagint, it being the word by which they translate the פקיד pakid of the Hebrew text, which signifies a visiter, one that personally inspects the people or business over which he presides. It is given by St. Paul to the elders at Ephesus, who had the oversight of Christ's flock, <reference osisRef="Act.20.28">Act 20:28</reference>; and to such like persons in other places, <reference osisRef="Phi.1.1">Phi 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Tim 3:2</reference>, the place in question; and <reference osisRef="Tit.1.7">Tit 1:7</reference>. <div eID="gen51627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51628" type="x-p"/> Let us consider the qualifications of a Christian bishop, and then we shall soon discover who is fit for the office. <div eID="gen51628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51629" type="x-p"/> First - is Christian bishop must be blameless; ανεπιληπτον, a person against whom no evil can be proved; one who is everywhere invulnerable; for the word is a metaphor, taken from the case of an expert and skillful pugilist, who so defends every part of his body that it is impossible for his antagonist to give one hit. So this Christian bishop is one that has so conducted himself, as to put it out of the reach of any person to prove that he is either unsound in a single article of the Christian faith, or deficient in the fulfillment of any duty incumbent on a Christian. He must be irreprehensible; for how can he reprove that in others which they can reprove in him? <div eID="gen51629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51630" type="x-p"/> Second - must be the husband of one wife. He should be a married man, but he should be no polygamist; and have only one wife, i.e. one at a time. It does not mean that, if he has been married, and his wife die, he should never marry another. Some have most foolishly spiritualized this, and say, that by one wife the Church is intended! This silly quibbling needs no refutation. The apostle's meaning appears to be this: that he should not be a man who has divorced his wife and married another; nor one that has two wives at a time. It does not appear to have been any part of the apostle's design to prohibit second marriages, of which some have made such a serious business. But it is natural for some men to tithe mint and cummin in religion, while they neglect the weightier matters of the law. <div eID="gen51630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51631" type="x-p"/> Third - must be vigilant; νηφαλεον, from νη, not and πιω, to drink. Watchful; for as one who drinks is apt to sleep, so he who abstains from it is more likely to keep awake, and attend to his work and charge. A bishop has to watch over the Church, and watch for it; and this will require all his care and circumspection. Instead of νηφαλεον, many MSS. read νηφαλιον· this may be the better orthography, but makes no alteration in the sense. <div eID="gen51631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51632" type="x-p"/> Fourth - must be sober; σωφρονα, prudent or, according to the etymology of the word, from σως, sound, and φρην, mind, a man of a sound mind; having a good understanding, and the complete government of all his passions. A bishop should be a man of learning, of an extensive and well cultivated mind, dispassionate, prudent, and sedate. <div eID="gen51632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51633" type="x-p"/> Fifth - must be of good behavior; κοσμιον, orderly, decent, grave, and correct in the whole of his appearance, carriage, and conduct. The preceding term, σωφρονα, refers to the mind; this latter, κοσμιον, to the external manners. A clownish, rude, or boorish man should never have the rule of the Church of God; the sour, the sullen, and the boisterous should never be invested with a dignity which they would most infallibly disgrace. <div eID="gen51633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51634" type="x-p"/> Sixth - must be given to hospitality; φιλοξενον, literally, a lover of strangers; one who is ready to receive into his house and relieve every necessitous stranger. Hospitality, in those primitive times, was a great and necessary virtue; then there were few inns, or places of public entertainment; to those who were noted for benevolence the necessitous stranger had recourse. A Christian bishop, professing love to God and all mankind, preaching a religion, one half of the morality of which was included in, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself, would naturally be sought to by those who were in distress and destitute of friends. To enable them to entertain such, the Church over which they presided must have furnished them with the means. Such a bishop as St. Paul, who was often obliged to labor with his hands for his own support, could have little to give away. But there is a considerable difference between an apostolical bishop and an ecclesiastical bishop: the one was generally itinerant, the other comparatively local; the former had neither house nor home, the latter had both; the apostolical bishop had charge of the Church of Christ universally, the ecclesiastical bishop of the Churches in a particular district. Such should be addicted to hospitality, or works of charity; especially in these modern times, in which, besides the spiritualities, they possess the temporalities, of the Church. <div eID="gen51634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51635" type="x-p"/> Seventh - should be apt to teach; διδακτικον, one capable of teaching; not only wise himself, but ready to communicate his wisdom to others. One whose delight is, to instruct the ignorant and those who are out of the way. He must be a preacher; an able, zealous, fervent, and assiduous preacher. <div eID="gen51635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51636" type="x-p"/> He is no bishop who has health and strength, and yet seldom or never preaches; i.e. if he can preach - if he have the necessary gifts for the office. <div eID="gen51636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51637" type="x-p"/> In former times bishops wrote much and preached much; and their labors were greatly owned of God. No Church since the apostle's days has been more honored in this way than the British Church.
